bush-tucker.name: Bush tucker
bush-tucker.summary: Native Australian foods historically eaten by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, including kangaroo, emu, and native fruits and yams.

witchetty-grub.name: Witchetty grub
witchetty-grub.summary: Large, white, wood-eating moth larvae eaten in Australia, historically a staple food in the diets of Aboriginal Australians.

quandong.name: Quandong
quandong.summary: Common name mainly for Santalum acuminatum, a desert tree species valued especially for its edible fruit.

tetragonia-tetragonioides.name: Warrigal greens
tetragonia-tetragonioides.summary: A leafy flowering plant native to eastern Asia, Australia and New Zealand, often cultivated as a vegetable; it grows well on sandy, salty coastal ground.

fire-stick-farming.name: Fire-stick farming
fire-stick-farming.summary: Cultural burning practice used by Aboriginal Australians for thousands of years to manage vegetation, aid hunting, and increase biodiversity.

kunzea-pomifera.name: Muntries
kunzea-pomifera.summary: Low-growing flowering shrub with edible fruit, endemic to south-east Australia, also called emu apples or native cranberries.

syzygium-luehmannii.name: Riberry
syzygium-luehmannii.summary: The fruit of a medium-sized rainforest tree native to coastal Australia, also called the small-leaved lilly pilly, grown for food and as an ornamental.

tasmannia-lanceolata.name: Mountain pepper
tasmannia-lanceolata.summary: A flowering shrub native to southeastern Australia, also called mountain pepper or native pepper, whose berries are used as a bush food spice.

araucaria-bidwillii.name: Bunya pine
araucaria-bidwillii.summary: A large coniferous tree native to southeast Queensland, Australia, with a tallest known individual of 51.5 metres in Bunya Mountains National Park.

torres-strait-islanders.name: Torres Strait Islanders
torres-strait-islanders.summary: Indigenous Melanesian peoples of the Torres Strait Islands, ethnically distinct from Aboriginal Australians, known for a seafaring culture and strong traditions in sculpture and mask-making.

malleefowl.name: Malleefowl
malleefowl.summary: Stocky, chicken-sized Australian ground bird known for the large nesting mounds males build and for giving no care to chicks after they hatch.

fistulina-hepatica.name: Beefsteak fungus
fistulina-hepatica.summary: An edible bracket fungus that visually resembles a slab of meat, found in Europe, Africa, Australia and North America.

tasman-district.name: Tasman District
tasman-district.summary: A local government district in the northwest of New Zealand's South Island, formed in 1989 from the former Tasman District and Golden Bay County.

m-ori-history.name: Archaic and Classic periods
m-ori-history.summary: Two eras of early Māori history: the Archaic period (c. 1300–c. 1500) and the following Classic period (c. 1500–1769), when population growth spurred more elaborate art and a new warrior culture with fortified pā.

didgeridoo.name: Didgeridoo
didgeridoo.summary: Wind instrument usually 1 to 3 metres long, with longer ones giving lower pitch. It is now played around the world but is still most strongly linked with Indigenous Australian music.

circular-breathing.name: Circular breathing
circular-breathing.summary: Technique used by players of some wind instruments to produce a continuous tone. The player breathes in through the nose while pushing out air stored in the cheeks.

yol-u.name: Yolŋu
yol-u.summary: Aboriginal Australian people of north-eastern Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory, whose clans belong to either the Dhuwa or Yirritja moiety.

arnhem-land.name: Arnhem Land
arnhem-land.summary: A remote region of Australia's Northern Territory, named after a Dutch ship in 1623 and home mostly to Aboriginal Australians, many living in small communities with little Western influence.

whakairo.name: Whakairo
whakairo.summary: Traditional Māori art of carving in wood, stone or bone.

m-ori-traditional-textiles.name: Raranga
m-ori-traditional-textiles.summary: Māori plaiting technique used to make baskets and mats, one of three main weaving methods alongside whatu and whiri. Weavers were mostly women, often trained in Te Whare Pora, the House of Weaving.

moriori.name: Moriori
moriori.summary: Polynesian people who settled New Zealand's Chatham Islands by around 1500 AD, developing a distinct culture and a pacifist tradition before being decimated by invaders in the 1830s.

chatham-islands.name: Chatham Islands
chatham-islands.summary: A Pacific archipelago about 800 km east of New Zealand, first settled by the Moriori and later invaded by Māori groups in 1835.

kakadu-national-park.name: Kakadu National Park
kakadu-national-park.summary: Large World Heritage protected area in Australia's Northern Territory, southeast of Darwin. Aboriginal owners manage it jointly with Parks Australia, and it holds rich rock art and varied wildlife.

tapu-polynesian-culture.name: Tapu
tapu-polynesian-culture.summary: A Polynesian concept of something holy or sacred involving rules and prohibitions; the source of the English word "taboo", from Captain Cook's 1777 visit to Tonga.

tohunga.name: Tohunga
tohunga.summary: In Māori culture, an expert practitioner of a skill or art, such as a priest, healer, navigator, carver, or teacher, sometimes also a family head or chief.

atua.name: Atua
atua.summary: Polynesian word for "power" or "strength," used for the gods and spirits of peoples such as the Māori and Hawaiians, originating in pre-Christian myths and legends.

tairua.name: Tairua
tairua.summary: Beachside town on the east coast of the Coromandel Peninsula in New Zealand's North Island, about 150 km east of Auckland. Its Māori name means 'two tides'.

wairau-bar.name: Wairau Bar
wairau-bar.summary: A gravel bar in New Zealand's South Island settled by East Polynesian explorers around 1280, one of the earliest known human settlement sites in the country.

society-islands.name: Society Islands
society-islands.summary: An archipelago in Polynesia in the South Pacific, part of French Polynesia, whose largest island is Tahiti; settlers from here later helped populate other Pacific islands.

p.name: Pā
p.summary: A Māori word for a fortified village or hillfort with palisades and terraces, built to protect food supplies; over 5,000 such sites have been found in New Zealand.

iwi.name: Iwi
iwi.summary: The largest social units in Māori society, often translated as 'tribe,' tracing ancestry to Polynesian migrants and still holding major political and economic influence in New Zealand.

rangatira.name: Rangatira
rangatira.summary: In Māori culture, a tribal chief who led a hapū (subtribe), traditionally holding mana on behalf of the tribe and maintaining its land boundaries.

kupe.name: Kupe
kupe.summary: Polynesian explorer credited in Māori history with being the first to discover New Zealand, around 1000–1300 CE, making him central to the origins of the Māori people.

kuram-r-tini.name: Kuramārōtini
kuram-r-tini.summary: Figure in Māori mythology, daughter of chief Toto, who sailed to New Zealand with the explorer Kupe after he tricked her husband Hoturapa overboard; said by some to have named the land Aotearoa.

matahourua.name: Matahourua
matahourua.summary: In Māori tradition, the canoe of the legendary explorer Kupe, said in some accounts to have discovered Aotearoa (New Zealand).

hawaiki.name: Hawaiki
hawaiki.summary: In Polynesian folklore, the original homeland of the Polynesians before their dispersal across the Pacific, also featured as an underworld in Māori stories.

tainui.name: Tainui
tainui.summary: A confederation of Māori tribes in New Zealand's central North Island, made up of the Hauraki, Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Raukawa and Waikato peoples.

te-arawa.name: Te Arawa
te-arawa.summary: A confederation of Māori tribes tracing their ancestry to the Arawa migration canoe, based around Rotorua and the Bay of Plenty in New Zealand.

aotea-canoe.name: Aotea
aotea-canoe.summary: One of the canoes in which, according to Māori tradition, Māori migrated to New Zealand, particularly associated with the Taranaki and Whanganui tribes.

m-taatua.name: Mātaatua
m-taatua.summary: One of the legendary voyaging canoes said to have brought Polynesian ancestors to New Zealand, according to Māori tradition; several Māori tribes trace their descent from its crew.

songline.name: Songline
songline.summary: A path across the land, recorded in song, story, dance and art, that Aboriginal Australian belief holds was followed by ancestral creator-beings.

whakapapa.name: Whakapapa
whakapapa.summary: The Māori concept of genealogy, central to identity, connecting people to land, ancestors, and tribal groups through recited lineages.

tamanuiter.name: Tama-nui-te-rā
tamanuiter.summary: In Māori mythology, the personification of the sun.

tane-rore.name: Tāne-rore
tane-rore.summary: Personification of shimmering air in Māori mythology, said to perform a haka for his mother, the Summer Maid Hine-raumati.

haka.name: Haka
haka.summary: A ceremonial Polynesian dance performed by groups with vigorous movements and chanted accompaniment, traditionally used for welcomes, celebrations or funerals, and made globally known through New Zealand rugby.

te-wheke-a-muturangi.name: Te Wheke-a-Muturangi
te-wheke-a-muturangi.summary: A monstrous octopus in Māori mythology, a pet of the sorcerer Muturangi, said to have been destroyed by the navigator Kupe after a great battle.

david-simmons-ethnologist.name: David Simmons
david-simmons-ethnologist.summary: New Zealand ethnologist, historian and author (1930–2015).

uluru.name: Uluru
uluru.summary: Large sandstone monolith in central Australia, sacred to the Aboriginal Pitjantjatjara people and a UNESCO World Heritage Site; one of Australia's most recognisable natural landmarks.

kata-tjuta.name: Kata Tjuta
kata-tjuta.summary: A group of large domed rock formations in central Australia's Northern Territory, also called The Olgas, sacred to the local Aboriginal community and part of Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park.

m-ui-m-ori-mythology.name: Māui
m-ui-m-ori-mythology.summary: In Māori tradition, a demigod trickster credited with catching the giant fish that became New Zealand's North Island using a fishhook made from his grandmother's jawbone.

north-island.name: Te Ika-a-Māui
north-island.summary: Māori name for the North Island of New Zealand, the country's most populous island, separated from the South Island by Cook Strait.

ka-mate.name: Ka Mate
ka-mate.summary: Māori haka composed by Te Rauparaha, the historic leader of Ngāti Toa in New Zealand's North Island during the Musket Wars.

moa.name: Moa
moa.summary: An extinct group of flightless birds unique to New Zealand, with the largest species standing 3.6 meters tall; hunted to extinction within about a century of Polynesian settlement.

polynesian-navigation.name: Wayfinding
polynesian-navigation.summary: Traditional Polynesian navigation techniques for long ocean voyages, using the stars, ocean swells, wind patterns and bird behavior, passed down through oral tradition rather than instruments.

maramataka.name: Maramataka
maramataka.summary: A Māori lunar calendar of twelve months, traditionally used to time activities such as fishing, eeling and planting according to the phases of the moon.

enderby-island.name: Enderby Island
enderby-island.summary: Uninhabited island in New Zealand's Auckland Islands archipelago, near the northern tip of Auckland Island itself, south of the New Zealand mainland.

auckland-islands.name: Auckland Islands
auckland-islands.summary: Uninhabited archipelago of New Zealand about 465 km south of the South Island, part of the New Zealand Subantarctic Islands UNESCO World Heritage Site.

upland-moa.name: Upland moa
upland-moa.summary: An extinct flightless bird native to New Zealand's South Island, favoring alpine areas, hunted by the Māori to extinction around 1500 CE.

rakaia-river.name: Rakaia River
rakaia-river.summary: One of the largest braided rivers in New Zealand's South Island, its Māori name meaning 'the place where people were arranged by ranks'.

arawa-canoe.name: Arawa (canoe)
arawa-canoe.summary: One of the great ocean-going canoes in Māori tradition used in the migrations that settled New Zealand; several Māori groups trace their ancestry to its people.

ngahue.name: Ngahue
ngahue.summary: A figure in Māori mythology, contemporary of Kupe and one of the first Polynesian explorers to reach New Zealand, credited with discovering pounamu (greenstone).

pei-te-hurinui-jones.name: Pei Te Hurinui Jones
pei-te-hurinui-jones.summary: Māori political leader, writer and historian (1898–1976) who led the Tainui confederation and King Movement, negotiated over land seizures, and wrote the first history of the Tainui people.

waikato.name: Waikato
waikato.summary: A region of New Zealand's upper North Island centered on the Waikato River, governed by the Waikato Regional Council and the country's fourth largest region by area and population.

hap.name: Hapū
hap.summary: A subtribe or clan that served as the basic political unit within Māori society; each hapū traditionally had its own chief and normally operated independently of its wider tribe.

wh-nau.name: Whānau
wh-nau.summary: The Māori word for an extended family group spanning three or four generations, forming the political unit below the hapū (subtribe) and iwi (tribe).

papanui-inlet.name: Papanui Inlet
papanui-inlet.summary: One of two large inlets on the Pacific coast of New Zealand's Otago Peninsula, named from Māori words for 'large flat area' and known for its diverse bird life.

waitaha-south-island-iwi.name: Waitaha
waitaha-south-island-iwi.summary: An early Māori iwi of New Zealand's South Island, largely absorbed through marriage and conquest by the Ngāti Māmoe and then Ngāi Tahu from the 16th century onward.

t-moko.name: Tā moko
t-moko.summary: Traditional Māori tattooing practice, one of the five main Polynesian tattoo styles, performed by tattooists considered sacred.

waka-canoe.name: Waka (canoe)
waka-canoe.summary: Māori watercraft ranging from small plain canoes to large carved war canoes (waka taua) up to 40 metres long; the earliest known New Zealand example dates to about 1400.

haast-s-eagle.name: Haast's eagle
haast-s-eagle.summary: An extinct eagle of New Zealand's South Island, the largest eagle known to have existed at 10 to 18 kilograms, which preyed on the flightless moa until it vanished around 1445.

sweet-potato.name: Kūmara
sweet-potato.summary: A starchy, sweet-tasting root vegetable native to tropical South America, a staple food in many regions and only distantly related to the true potato.
